title: Book 02 — Chapter 2, Session 1: Revised Exam Questions and Model Answers

source.title: Chapter 2: Imam al-Hasan’s Pacifism (Session 1)
source.author: Ayatullah Murtadha Mutahhari
source.method: Questions were checked against the original Session 1 source. The answer bank distinguishes the jurisprudential categories of jihad, the conditions for peace, and the historical examples of the Prophet and Imam ‘Ali.

revision_policy: Keep Session 1 focused on the general principles of jihad, peace, and Hudaybiyyah; Session 2 separately examines Imam al-Hasan’s historical circumstances and treaty.
Distinguish antecedent jihad, defensive jihad, self-defence, fighting rebels, and armed uprising for enjoining good.
State the conditions for truce, including benefit to Muslims and a definite term.
Use the Prophet’s and Imam ‘Ali’s examples to show that peace and fighting depend on circumstances.

questions.prompt: What broader question does Mutahhari raise when examining Imam al-Hasan’s peace and Imam al-Husayn’s uprising?
questions.answer: Mutahhari asks whether the different actions of Imam al-Hasan and Imam al-Husayn arose from different personal temperaments or from the different circumstances of their times. He rejects the idea that one Imam was naturally peace-seeking while the other was inherently rebellious. Instead, he argues that both acted according to their religious duties and the conditions they faced. To understand their decisions, he first examines the Islamic principles governing jihad, defence, resistance, reconciliation, and peace. The central question is therefore not whether Islam is simply a religion of peace or war, but when each response is required or permitted.
questions.source_locator: Opening question — Why did Imam al-Hasan make peace while Imam al-Husayn resisted?

questions.prompt: Why did the Prophet not permit Muslims to fight during the early years of his mission in Mecca, despite their suffering persecution?
questions.answer: Mutahhari explains that Muslims were tortured and some were killed during the thirteen years in Mecca, and some companions asked the Prophet for permission to fight. He did not grant permission; at most, he allowed some Muslims to migrate to Abyssinia. Permission to fight was granted after the migration to Medina, when the Qur’anic verse permitting the oppressed to defend themselves was revealed. The example shows that severe suffering alone did not automatically determine the form of response. The Prophet acted according to the stage of the mission and the circumstances of the Muslim community.
questions.source_locator: The Holy Prophet and peace — Why the Prophet sometimes fought and sometimes made peace

questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari answer the question of whether Islam is a religion of peace or a religion of war?
questions.answer: Mutahhari rejects both absolute positions. Islam does not require peace in every circumstance, nor does it require fighting in every circumstance. The Qur’an contains commands relating to fighting and also commands to accept peace when the opposing side inclines toward it. The correct course depends on the circumstances and the interests and rights of the Muslim community. The Prophet sometimes fought, sometimes made peace with enemies, and also signed agreements with groups such as the Jews of Medina. Mutahhari concludes that peace and war are both legitimate in their proper contexts; neither should be treated as an unchanging rule detached from circumstances.
questions.source_locator: The Holy Prophet and peace — Why the Prophet sometimes fought and sometimes made peace

questions.prompt: What examples does Mutahhari give of the Prophet making peace even with opponents?
questions.answer: Mutahhari mentions the Prophet’s peace treaty at Hudaybiyyah with the Quraysh, who were among the Muslims’ strongest enemies. He also refers to a non-aggression agreement with the Jews of Medina. These examples show that the Prophet did not regard fighting as the only response to hostility. Even when companions were unhappy with the terms, he accepted a treaty when it served a greater purpose for the Muslim community. The examples support Mutahhari’s argument that peace can be a principled and strategic choice rather than a sign of weakness or surrender.
questions.source_locator: The Holy Prophet and peace — Why the Prophet sometimes fought and sometimes made peace

questions.prompt: How did Imam ‘Ali respond when the question of succession arose after the Prophet’s death?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that when others took the position of succession after the Prophet, Imam ‘Ali refrained from fighting and did not draw his sword. He explained that his duty at that time was restraint, even though he had the courage and ability to fight. Lady Fatimah objected to his withdrawal, asking why the man who had been fearless in battle was now sitting quietly while others had taken control. ‘Ali answered that his duty in the earlier circumstances had been to fight, while his duty in the present circumstances was different. Mutahhari uses this example to show that an Imam’s method must be judged by the circumstances and religious responsibility of the time.
questions.source_locator: ‘Ali and peace — Restraint, mediation, and arbitration under pressure

questions.prompt: What role did Imam ‘Ali play during the uprising against ‘Uthman?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that Imam ‘Ali was not among the rebels against ‘Uthman. Instead, he acted as a mediator between the rebels and the caliph, trying to address their legitimate complaints about an oppressive governor while preventing ‘Uthman from being killed. ‘Ali warned ‘Uthman that if he were murdered, killing would become an accepted political method and a rebellion might arise among Muslims that would be difficult to suppress. Mutahhari presents this as another example of ‘Ali choosing mediation and restraint when that was the duty required by the circumstances.
questions.source_locator: ‘Ali and peace — Restraint, mediation, and arbitration under pressure

questions.prompt: How did Imam ‘Ali’s policy change after ‘Uthman’s death and his own assumption of the caliphate?
questions.answer: After ‘Uthman’s death, people pledged allegiance to Imam ‘Ali, and he became the caliph. He then fought against groups that rebelled against his just government: the Violators, the Deviators, and those who departed from the truth, associated with the battles of Jamal, Siffin, and Nahrawan. Mutahhari uses this change to show that ‘Ali did not avoid fighting as a matter of personal temperament. When he held the responsibility of government and faced groups rebelling against a just Imam, his duty was to defend the legitimate order and confront those who refused reconciliation.
questions.source_locator: ‘Ali and peace — Restraint, mediation, and arbitration under pressure

questions.prompt: Why did Imam ‘Ali accept arbitration after the Battle of Siffin?
questions.answer: Mutahhari explains that after Siffin, the Kharijites created division within Imam ‘Ali’s army, while Mu‘awiyah and ‘Amr ibn al-‘As raised copies of the Qur’an on spears and called for arbitration. Some of ‘Ali’s own soldiers accepted the proposal and pressured him to agree. He therefore accepted arbitration based on the Qur’an and Islamic commandments, although the process was later manipulated by ‘Amr ibn al-‘As. Mutahhari presents the decision as another example of accepting a peaceful or conciliatory process under particular circumstances, not as proof that ‘Ali abandoned his principles or accepted Mu‘awiyah’s legitimacy.
questions.source_locator: ‘Ali and peace — Restraint, mediation, and arbitration under pressure

questions.prompt: What are the five broad cases of jihad that Mutahhari discusses in this session?
questions.answer: Mutahhari discusses antecedent or offensive jihad; defensive jihad when Muslim territory, people, property, or sanctities are attacked; particular cases of self-defence and protection of life or property that carry the reward of martyrdom but do not necessarily share all the legal rules of general jihad; fighting rebels when one group oppresses another and refuses reconciliation; and armed uprisings for enjoining good and forbidding evil, which have their own levels and are subject to scholarly disagreement. The categories have different conditions, permissions, and legal consequences. They must not be collapsed into one undifferentiated concept of fighting.
questions.source_locator: The cases for jihad in the Shi‘ah jurisprudence

questions.prompt: What is antecedent jihad, and what authorization does it require in Shi‘ah jurisprudence as described by Mutahhari?
questions.answer: Antecedent jihad is the type of jihad in which Muslims may initiate fighting against non-Muslims, particularly polytheists, even when there has been no prior record of hostility between the two sides. Mutahhari says that this form of jihad has specific conditions: it is restricted to adult, sane, free male soldiers, and in Shi‘ah jurisprudence it requires the permission of an Imam or someone personally appointed by an Imam. He emphasizes that even a religious leader who has not been authorized by the Imam cannot initiate this type of war. This is distinct from defensive jihad, which does not require the Imam’s permission.
questions.source_locator: The cases for jihad in the Shi‘ah jurisprudence — Offensive jihad and authorization

questions.prompt: When does defensive jihad become obligatory, and who is required to participate?
questions.answer: Defensive jihad becomes obligatory when an enemy attacks Muslim territory or threatens the lives, property, families, children, or other sanctities of Muslims. Mutahhari says that this obligation is not restricted to adult free men or to the people living in the directly attacked area. It can apply to men and women, free and non-free people, and Muslims near or far, if their assistance is needed. Unlike antecedent jihad, defensive jihad does not require the permission of the Imam or his representative. The obligation becomes stronger for those who are geographically closer, and it applies when the attacked community does not have sufficient strength to defend itself.
questions.source_locator: The cases for jihad in the Shi‘ah jurisprudence — Defense against an attack

questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari distinguish the particular cases of self-defence from general jihad?
questions.answer: Mutahhari describes situations in which a person living outside an Islamic land is caught in a war between non-Muslim powers, or in which an attacker threatens a person’s life, family, or property. A Muslim may have to defend himself even if the conflict is not a general jihad against an enemy of Islam. If killed in such circumstances, the person may receive the reward of a martyr, but the special legal rules of general jihad—such as burial without washing in the clothing of martyrdom—do not necessarily apply. Mutahhari’s distinction is between the moral reward for defending oneself and the technical legal status and rules of general jihad.
questions.source_locator: The cases for jihad in the Shi‘ah jurisprudence — Personal defense and differing levels of risk

questions.prompt: What differing levels of risk does Mutahhari mention when defending property, life, and family?
questions.answer: Mutahhari distinguishes defending property from defending life and family. When a thief attacks a person’s property, he says that resistance is obligatory even when the chance of death is relatively small, and that a person may continue resisting while the chance of survival remains at least fifty percent. When the threat is to one’s own life or the life of relatives, the obligation to resist is stronger: even if the chance of being killed is certain, the person must defend against the attacker. The example shows that the legal and moral duty depends on what is being threatened, not merely on the general fact that violence is present.
questions.source_locator: The cases for jihad in the Shi‘ah jurisprudence — Personal defense and differing levels of risk

questions.prompt: What is the rule for fighting rebels when a conflict breaks out between two Muslim groups?
questions.answer: Mutahhari explains that when two Muslim groups fight and one wrongs the other, the first responsibility of the wider Muslim community is to reconcile them and establish peace. If one side refuses reconciliation and continues to oppress the other, it becomes obligatory to fight the rebellious group in support of the oppressed side until it returns to Allah’s command. He cites Qur’an 49:9, which instructs believers to make peace between disputing groups and then fight the wrongful party if it persists in aggression. One application is defending a just Imam against people who rebel against him.
questions.source_locator: Fighting rebels — Reconciliation before confronting the wrongful side

questions.prompt: What does Mutahhari say about armed uprisings for enjoining good and forbidding evil?
questions.answer: Mutahhari identifies bloody uprisings undertaken for enjoining good and forbidding evil as a further category that has its own stages and conditions. He notes that scholars have differed over this issue and that it cannot simply be treated as identical to defensive jihad or fighting rebels. The category concerns the use of force to oppose serious wrongdoing and restore religious and moral order. Mutahhari’s point is that it must be examined through its own jurisprudential rules rather than assumed to be obligatory or permissible in every situation.
questions.source_locator: Fighting rebels — Reconciliation before confronting the wrongful side

questions.prompt: Under what conditions is a peace treaty or truce permissible in Shi‘ah jurisprudence, according to the passage Mutahhari cites?
questions.answer: Mutahhari quotes the jurist Muhaqqiq al-Hilli to explain that a truce is permissible when it benefits the Muslims. The benefit may arise because the Muslims are too few or too weak to resist the enemy, because the truce gives them time to obtain reinforcements and become stronger, or because the period of peace may create an opportunity for the opposing non-Muslims to accept Islam. If the Muslims are already strong enough to overcome the enemy and the truce offers no benefit, it is not permissible. The decision must therefore be based on the interests of the Muslim community and the circumstances of the conflict.
questions.source_locator: Peace in the Shi‘ah jurisprudence — When a time-limited truce is permitted

questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari say that a peace treaty must specify a definite period rather than remain indefinite?
questions.answer: Mutahhari explains that a truce is an agreement to cease fighting for a specified period. It should not be an indefinite arrangement described only as peace “for the time being.” A definite duration—such as six months, one year, or ten years—makes the agreement clear and prevents a temporary ceasefire from becoming an open-ended surrender. He cites the Prophet’s treaty of Hudaybiyyah, which was set for ten years, as an example. The time limit also allows the Muslims to use the period for recovery, reinforcement, or the spiritual attraction of the opposing community.
questions.source_locator: Peace in the Shi‘ah jurisprudence — When a time-limited truce is permitted

questions.prompt: Explain how the Prophet’s actions demonstrate that Islam permits both fighting and peace according to the circumstances.
questions.answer: Mutahhari points to the Prophet’s thirteen years in Mecca, during which Muslims were tortured and killed but were not permitted to fight. Some were allowed to migrate to Abyssinia. Permission to fight came after the migration to Medina, when the Qur’anic verse allowing the oppressed to defend themselves was revealed. Even after that, the Prophet did not fight in every situation: he fought in some circumstances, signed agreements with the Jews of Medina, and accepted the treaty of Hudaybiyyah with the Quraysh despite the dissatisfaction of many companions. These examples show that Islam is neither absolutely pacifist nor permanently warlike. The proper response depends on the circumstances, the rights of Muslims, the possibility of achieving a just outcome, and the interests served by fighting or peace.
questions.source_locator: The Holy Prophet and peace — Why the Prophet sometimes fought and sometimes made peace

questions.prompt: Trace the different stages of Imam ‘Ali’s use of restraint, mediation, fighting, and arbitration, and explain what they demonstrate.
questions.answer: After the Prophet’s death, when the issue of succession was taken away from him, Imam ‘Ali refrained from fighting and explained that his duty in those circumstances was restraint. During the following twenty-five years, he acted as a conciliator and mediated between ‘Uthman and the people who had legitimate complaints against one of his governors. After ‘Uthman’s death and ‘Ali’s own assumption of the caliphate, people pledged allegiance to him, and he fought the groups that rebelled against his just government in the battles of Jamal, Siffin, and Nahrawan. After Siffin, when division in his own army and the Qur’an-on-spears stratagem forced the issue, he accepted arbitration. Mutahhari uses these stages to show that ‘Ali’s actions were not determined by a fixed personal preference for peace or war. His response changed according to his role, the conduct of opponents, and the responsibilities of the time.
questions.source_locator: ‘Ali and peace — Restraint, mediation, and arbitration under pressure

questions.prompt: Explain the different cases of jihad discussed by Mutahhari and why each has distinct legal conditions.
questions.answer: Mutahhari distinguishes several forms of jihad. Antecedent jihad is an initiated campaign against non-Muslims and, in Shi‘ah jurisprudence, requires the Imam’s permission and is restricted to qualified men. Defensive jihad becomes obligatory when Muslim land, people, property, or sanctities are attacked; it does not require the Imam’s permission and can apply to the whole community if assistance is needed. Particular cases of self-defence arise when a person’s life, family, or property is attacked, or when a Muslim is caught in a war between non-Muslim states; the reward may be that of a martyr, but not all legal rules of general jihad apply. Fighting rebels requires first attempting reconciliation between Muslim groups, then fighting the wrongful party if it refuses peace. Finally, armed uprisings for enjoining good and forbidding evil form a separate category with levels and scholarly disagreement. The distinctions show that jihad is not one undifferentiated obligation; its rules depend on the cause, authority, threat, and purpose.
questions.source_locator: The cases for jihad in the Shi‘ah jurisprudence

questions.prompt: What is the jurisprudential basis for self-defence, and how does Mutahhari distinguish the defence of property from the defence of life?
questions.answer: Mutahhari explains that a person must defend himself when an attacker threatens his life, family, or property, even if the attacker is a Muslim. The degree of obligation differs according to what is at risk. In the case of property, resistance is obligatory when there is a reasonable chance of survival, and the person may continue while the chance of survival remains at least fifty percent. If the attacker threatens the person’s life or the lives of family members, the duty to resist is stronger and remains even if the chance of being killed is certain. The point is that a person cannot simply submit to an attacker and say that the attacker intends to kill him. Islam recognizes a duty to protect life and family, while also distinguishing the degree of risk involved in defending property.
questions.source_locator: The cases for jihad in the Shi‘ah jurisprudence — Personal defense and differing levels of risk

questions.prompt: Explain the conditions under which peace or truce is permitted in Shi‘ah jurisprudence and why a treaty without benefit may be impermissible.
questions.answer: Mutahhari cites Muhaqqiq al-Hilli’s explanation that peace is a time-limited agreement to cease fighting. It is permissible when it serves the interests of the Muslims. This may be because the Muslims are too few or weak to resist, because the truce allows them to obtain assistance and reinforcements, or because it creates an opportunity for the opposing non-Muslims to embrace Islam. The treaty must specify a definite duration rather than remain indefinite. If the Muslims are sufficiently strong to defeat the enemy and the truce offers no benefit, then a truce is not permissible. Mutahhari also distinguishes a formal peace treaty from a broader period of peaceful coexistence when Muslims are too weak to resist. In both cases, the decision must be judged by its purpose and consequences for the community, not by a fixed assumption that peace is always right or always wrong.
questions.source_locator: Peace in the Shi‘ah jurisprudence — When a time-limited truce is permitted

questions.prompt: Describe the events of Hudaybiyyah and explain why the Prophet accepted conditions that appeared unfavourable to the Muslims.
questions.answer: In the sixth year after Hijrah, the Prophet set out for Mecca with a group of companions intending to perform pilgrimage, not to fight. Mutahhari gives the number as about seven hundred, while other reports say fourteen hundred, and mentions that seventy sacrificial camels were sent ahead to show that the Muslims were pilgrims. The Quraysh refused to allow them to enter Mecca, and messengers were exchanged. The Prophet repeatedly explained that he had come only for pilgrimage and was willing to make peace. Suhayl ibn ‘Amr eventually negotiated a treaty under which the Muslims would return to Medina and come back the following year for three days. Some clauses appeared unfavourable, including the requirement to return certain Quraysh members who joined the Muslims. The Prophet accepted the conditions because the treaty would give Muslims freedom from pressure in Mecca and allow them to preach Islam. Within less than a year, many more people accepted Islam than had done so in the preceding twenty years. Mutahhari presents Hudaybiyyah as proof that an apparently unfavourable treaty can serve a much greater religious purpose.
questions.source_locator: Hudaybiyyah Peace — Why a seemingly unfavourable treaty could serve a greater aim

questions.prompt: What do the stories of Abu Jandal and Abu Basir reveal about the Prophet’s commitment to the Hudaybiyyah treaty and its eventual outcome?
questions.answer: After the treaty was signed, Abu Jandal, the son of Suhayl ibn ‘Amr, escaped from the Quraysh and sought refuge with the Muslims. Because the agreement required the return of certain Quraysh members who came to Medina, the Prophet returned him despite the distress of the companions. The Prophet explained that the Muslims had made an agreement and must honour it, while assuring the oppressed that God would open a way for them. Abu Basir later escaped from Mecca and was returned under the treaty, but after an incident with his guards he established a base near the Red Sea. Other persecuted Muslims gradually joined him, and the community grew strong enough that the Quraysh asked the Prophet to release them from the return clause. These events show that the Prophet honoured the treaty even when its terms were painful, and that the period of peace ultimately created freedom and strength for the Muslims.
questions.source_locator: Hudaybiyyah Peace — Why a seemingly unfavourable treaty could serve a greater aim

questions.prompt: What is Mutahhari’s overall conclusion about the relationship between peace, war, and the duties of the Imams?
questions.answer: Mutahhari concludes that Islam does not treat peace or war as an absolute principle that must be applied regardless of circumstances. The Qur’an contains instructions for fighting, accepting peace, and reconciliation. The Prophet sometimes refrained from fighting in Mecca, sometimes fought in Medina, and sometimes signed treaties such as Hudaybiyyah. Imam ‘Ali also moved between restraint, mediation, fighting, and arbitration according to the situation. The jurisprudential discussion shows that different forms of jihad and peace have different conditions. The main objective must always be the preservation of Islam and the rights of Muslims. Therefore, Imam al-Hasan’s peace and Imam al-Husayn’s uprising cannot be judged by a simple rule that one response is always correct. Each must be assessed according to the circumstances and the religious responsibility of the time.
questions.source_locator: Opening question — Why did Imam al-Hasan make peace while Imam al-Husayn resisted?
